items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: We prove that the smooth affine hypersurfaces \[ X_{m,n}=\{ζ^mz_0^n+ (1+z_1ζ)z_2+ζz_3^2=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}^5,\;\; m,n\geq 2, \] have the density property. For every odd integer $d\geq 3$, we identify $X_{d-1,d}$ with a Kaliman modification along a Brieskorn variety of type $(d,2,2,2)$. We prove that the fourfolds $X_{d-1,d}$ are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$ but not biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$. These, therefore, give counterexamples to the Tóth-Varolin conjecture.
items.title: A new class of smooth algebraic varieties with the density property and a counterexample to the Tóth-Varolin Conjecture

items.summary: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second, approximately up to 136 times faster than GMR and ProtoMotions, while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.
items.title: Fast Motion Retargeting Pipeline for Scalable Humanoid Robot Learning

items.summary: Reliable video perception over bandwidth-constrained wireless links requires transmitting information that the receiver cannot already recover from its evolving scene representation. This paper introduces WorldGT, a world-model-guided semantic packet transmission framework that prioritizes information according to its contribution to the receiver's perception. A shared feature-space world model predicts the receiver's scene state through affine motion compensation and learned residual displacement, while sender-side verification identifies reusable predictions. An acknowledgment-synchronized receiver twin estimates task-impact scores through two counterfactual evaluations, guiding packet selection and unequal error protection over LDPC-coded wireless channels. A compact 3-bit feature representation increases spatial coverage under stringent bandwidth constraints, while predictive fallback sustains perception during packet outages. Experiments on KITTI and VisDrone under Rayleigh fading and AWGN demonstrate substantial gains in low-SNR conditions. On KITTI at a 4.13% reference bandwidth budget, WorldGT achieves 47.5% J&F at 0 dB Rayleigh SNR, outperforming H.264 by 11.3 percentage points. Controlled ablations show that world-model prediction contributes up to 8.7 points under Rayleigh fading. Object-detection experiments further demonstrate the transferability of receiver-relative predictive transmission across visual perception tasks. These results establish world-model-guided, receiver-state-aware transmission as an effective approach to robust video perception under severe communication constraints.
items.title: Guess and Send: World-Model-Guided Semantic Packet Transmission for Robust Video Perception

items.summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound;
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

items.summary: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.
items.title: A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: This archive provides the numerical models, processed experimental data, simulation results, statistical analyses, figure sources, and reproduction scripts associated with the study "Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation." The package includes OpenSeesPy model implementations, nonlinear earthquake-sequence analyses, measurement-resolution and model-discrepancy evaluations, experimental response comparisons, and modal-probe diagnostics. The archive is distributed in five ZIP parts. Download and extract all five parts into the same directory, preserving the internal folder structure. Reproduction instructions, dependencies, input provenance, and file-integrity verification are provided in README.md. Experimental measurements support validation of essentially elastic global response; nonlinear retrospective-state reconstruction is evaluated numerically.
items.title: Measurement limits and model discrepancy in reconstructing pre-earthquake residual deformation: Reproduction package

items.summary: Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch's FlexAttention. We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models.
items.title: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation

items.summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.
items.title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks

items.summary: This Zenodo record contains the public participant package for the FABEST High-Cycle Fatigue (HCF) Competition, a blind round-robin benchmark for fatigue-life prediction of 42CrMo4+QT steel under multiaxial high-cycle fatigue loading. Participants are asked to submit fatigue-life predictions for plain and notched hollow cylindrical specimens subjected to combined axial and torsional loading, including in-phase and 90° out-of-phase loading histories, with constant internal pressure. The package includes the competition rules, start-here guide, experimental basis, calibration data, public blind load matrix, specimen geometry information, manufacturing documentation, roughness and residual-stress characterisation, test setup and test-sequence descriptions, and participant submission templates. All files are provided as zipped folders to preserve the folder structure of the competition package.
items.title: FABEST High-Cycle Fatigue Competition: Participant Package for Blind Fatigue-Life Prediction

items.summary: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.
items.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion

items.summary: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation and Knowledge Transfer, represents the most significant recodification of the Czech RDI system in more than two decades. It replaces Act No. 130/2002 Coll., whose repeated amendments gradually reduced the clarity of the original framework and weakened its ability to respond to the changing needs of the research and innovation system. The Act constitutes a comprehensive reconstruction of the legal framework, complemented by Amending Act No. 329/2025 Coll. and implementing regulations. This article interprets the Act as a framework for a more investment-oriented governance of public support for RDI: in other words, as a basis for deciding how the state supports the creation, development and use of knowledge and innovation. Its key principle is the connection between excellence and impact. Excellent research is no longer treated as a value in itself, but as a precondition whose contribution must be demonstrable in terms of the country’s prosperity, security and international credibility. The Act therefore not only strengthens the capacity of research organisations to translate results into practice, but also opens space for instruments that may increase demand for knowledge, technologies and innovation. The text is not a legal commentary on the new legislation. Rather, it offers a sociological, historical and economic analysis that places the new legal framework within the broader context of the Czech RDI system. It is structured as a coherent arc: context – changes – implementation conditions – discussion – recommendations – conclusion.
items.title: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation, and Knowledge Transfer: Recodification of the R&D&I legal framework in the Czech Republic

items.summary: This is a simulated photoacoustic data set based on the Monte Carlo Method using the simulation framework SIMPA. The simulations use a literature-based forearm model (see Appendix D of Schellenberg et al., Photoacoustics 28, 2022 ) and a digital twin of the MSOT Acuity Echo (iThera Medical). The generating script performs volume generation and optical forward simulation in 3D with MCX using 10⁸ photons and a spacing of 0.1 mm for 16 wavelengths (700 - 850nm in steps of 10nm). Acoustic simulations were performed on the central slice using k-Wave. Images were reconstructed with SIMPA’s delay-and-sum reconstruction algorithm (1540 m/s speed of sound, Tukey windowed bandpass filtering (0.1 - 8 MHz), and Hilbert transform envelope detection.  It comprises 1243 multispectral images in total, each of size 200 x 400 px containing these eight channels: oxygen saturation segmentation with classes: muscle, heavy water, blood vessel, epidermis, US gel, mediprene absorption coefficient scattering coefficient scattering anisotropy fluence initial pressure distribution delay-and-sum reconstruction
items.title: Simulated multispectral photoacoustic forearm dataset with reference initial pressure, segmentation, and vessel oxygenation maps

items.summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
items.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
Reconstruction of the Neutrino Nature Based on the Great Tao Model and a Unified Explanation of Related Puzzles

items.summary: Pyralysis (PYthon Radio Astronomy anaLYSis and Image Synthesis) is an open-source Python library for radio-interferometric simulation, gridding, and image reconstruction. Imaging is stated as an explicit optimization problem — chi-squared (and closure / bispectrum terms) plus regularizers you choose — solved with modern first-order methods (e.g. FISTA, L-BFGS, SDMM). It is not a black-box CLEAN imager.
items.title: Pyralysis

items.summary: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
items.title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning

items.summary: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
items.title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI

items.summary: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.
items.title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits

items.summary: Nanoscale nonreciprocal elements are needed to control signal flow in scalable quantum technologies, but existing nonreciprocal components are often bulky. Here, we show that a strongly nonreciprocal current-voltage relation can arise entirely from coherent elastic scattering in a mesoscopic Rashba nanowire with gate-defined scatterers. We first identify the symmetry constraints that enforce reciprocal transmission in a phase coherent conductor even when inversion and time-reversal symmetry are broken. We then show how gates that are capacitively coupled to the leads, together with a magnetic scatterer or transverse subband mixing, can remove these constraints. In the weak-scattering regime, nonreciprocal conductance originates from interference between distinct backscattering paths. In the strong-scattering regime, nonreciprocity can be resonantly enhanced by the hybridization of the transmitting channel with bound states that arise from a higher transverse subband or spin-split band. In this regime, we find that a bias-induced change in the gate potentials of about one percent can produce an order-unity diode response, i.e., electrons are transmitted almost as in a clean wire for one bias polarity, whereas for the other polarity the current is strongly suppressed.
items.title: Quantum Interference Enhanced Rectification in Mesoscopic Nanowires

items.summary: This reproducible code and data documents substantial errors in the Science paper " The air pollution benefits of low-severity fire " (Higuera-Mendieta & Burke 2026), that, when corrected, reverse the core conclusions of the paper. You can find their code here: https://zenodo.org/records/20944436   Their paper uses low-severity wildfire as a proxy for prescribed fire to estimate the tradeoff between the smoke generated by treatment (the costs) and the smoke it avoids in future wildfires (the benefit). However, the analysis contains errors that 1) substantially overestimate benefits and 2) underestimate costs. Correcting these issues reverse the paper's reported air pollution benefits.  The analysis relies on two contradictory definitions of low-severity treatment that artificially inflate the benefit-cost tradeoff. The paper argues that low-severity wildfire (dNBR 100-270) is a valid proxy for prescribed fire when estimating treatment benefits, but then assumes that prescribed fire emits only ~15% as much smoke when estimating treatment costs (it assumes a much lower prescribed fire severity range of dNBR 10-40). Actual empirical ranges of MBTS-mapped prescribed fire in their focal landscapes have a mean fire severity of 133 dNBR. Correcting this issue (either using empirical MTBS dNBR ranges, or more appropriately, using an equivalent 100-270 dNBR low-severity fire range) reverses the findings of net air pollution benefits (their Figure 4 and Figure 5c).  The analysis of the benefit-cost ratio (their Figure 4) also demonstrably overestimates benefits by counting emissions reductions that are not physically possible. For example, their analysis often counts modeled reductions in dNBR that exceed the the observed dNBR in the grid cell (e.g., counting a reduction of 169 dNBR units of emissions when there are only 79 dNBR units of observed wildfire), and counts reductions in dNBR when there was no observable wildfire in the first place (e.g., observed dNBR < 0). Together, this error artificially inflates actual emissions reduction benefits of treatments.
items.title: Code and data to document substantial errors in "The air pollution benefits of low-severity fire" by Higuera-Mendieta & Burke (2026)

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
items.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing

items.summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
items.title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents

items.summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
items.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

items.summary: A hardening release from the 2026-10-21 full review ( docs/reviews/2026-10-21-full-review.md ): untrusted bundles and archives can no longer read or write outside themselves or exhaust memory, arkiv convert no longer destroys records, and malformed archives, bundles, and JSONL files report a clean error instead of a traceback (for crafted databases, only colliding asset rows are covered so far; see Known issues). No on-disk structure changes; arkiv_format stays "0.2" . Security S1: README contents entries (and schema.yaml , nested README files, and the archive's own README.md ) that are absolute, contain .. or a backslash, or resolve outside the archive are refused, so a crafted archive can no longer import arbitrary .jsonl files, or the text of any host file, from the host. S2: symlinks under media/ (including a symlinked media/ itself) are never followed or imported, so host files cannot land in the database and then in exported bundles. Directory import, the source fingerprint, and pack_bundle now share one walk ( iter_source_files ). S3: tar bundles are read with bounded headers: GNU long-name and pax headers over 1 MiB, or chained deeper than 8, are refused before they are read into memory, and sparse members are refused. A 65 KB archive no longer needs hundreds of MiB, and unpack_bundle is bounded too. S4: a database path containing # , ? , or % (or non-ASCII characters, or spaces) opens the file it names when opened read-only, instead of opening, and creating, a different file. S5: duplicate tar and zip members are refused on unpack, as are tar hard and symbolic links, FIFOs, and devices, so iter_jsonl and convert can no longer disagree about an archive's content. Names that differ only in case or Unicode normalization ( records.jsonl and Records.jsonl ) count as duplicates, since a case-insensitive filesystem (APFS, NTFS) stores them as one file. S6: MCP sql_query aborts after 10 seconds (an infinite recursive CTE no longer hangs the server) and cuts any text or blob cell over 100000 characters. S7: asset rows in a crafted database can no longer overwrite README.md , *.jsonl , or other non-media files on export; only canonical paths under media/ are written, checked on the resolved path. Fixed L1: arkiv convert <dir> after MCP write_record no longer silently deletes the written records; it refuses and names the export command. L2: reconverting a directory into its existing database rebuilds it from scratch, so collections, README text, and schema descriptions removed from the directory are gone from the database too, and status no longer reports in_sync over stale content. L3: records with a wrongly typed known field ( "metadata": null or a list, object or array content , list mimetype , boolean content ) no longer crash the import with a traceback or store "1" . L4: a high-cardinality key's example is stored apart from its enumerated values , so it is no longer written back as a bogus curated values: [id-0] ; a stale values from an earlier export heals on the next convert and export. C1: following the guard's advice ( arkiv convert x.db x ) now clears it; a full db-to-directory export records the directory and resets the unexported-writes counter. C5: a UTF-8 byte order mark no longer drops the first record of a JSONL file, in parse_jsonl , in the bundle readers, and in arkiv detect and arkiv fix (which keeps the mark when it rewrites the file). C6: zip packing no longer fails on a member of 2 GiB or more ( pack_bundle declares each member's size up front so zipfile switches to zip64 for members over 2 GiB), and write_bundle and pack_bundle write atomically, so a failure leaves no partial bundle behind. C7: corrupt, truncated, or encrypted bundles, and files that are not the archive their extension claims (a non-zip named .zip ), report a clean ValueError instead of a traceback ( zlib.error , NotImplementedError , RuntimeError , EOFError , BadZipFile , tarfile.ReadError ), in unpack

items.summary: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
items.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents

items.summary: We study inhomogeneous random graphs on $n$ vertices with independent Pareto weights of parameter $α>0$ and connection probabilities $\min(\varepsilon_n W_iW_j, 1)$. Our main focus is the infinite-mean regime $0<α<1$. Under the scaling $n\varepsilon_n^α=λ$, with $λ>0$ fixed, the global architecture of the graph is entirely governed by the Poisson point process $Π$ of rescaled extreme weights. In particular, the size of the largest component, divided by $n$, converges to a non-degenerate random variable expressed as an explicit functional of $Π$. Through the point process $Π$, we also characterize the exact limiting connectivity probability, uncovering a non-sharp connectivity threshold. The second largest component and the diameter of the largest component are bounded with high probability. The distance between two uniformly chosen vertices in the largest component is at most three with high probability. We also prove convergence of the point process of rescaled degrees and identify the limiting distribution of the maximum degree. For completeness, we obtain expected degree asymptotics, typical degree limits and connectivity regimes for all $α>0$. Due to the failure of classical branching process approximations in the infinite-mean regime, our approach relies fundamentally on analyzing the extreme weight environment $Π$.
items.title: Inhomogeneous random graphs: how heavy tails reshape connectivity

items.summary: Background:  Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the therapeutic landscape of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Beyond their primary glucose-lowering actions, both drug classes exert profound organ-protective effects. Objective:  This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on the molecular, cellular, and physiological mechanisms driving the cardio- and nephroprotective outcomes of SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs. Methods:  A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases following PRISMA guidelines for studies published between 2018 and 2026. Results:  SGLT2i act primarily via hemodynamic restoration, reducing intraglomerular pressure through tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF), shifting myocardial energetics toward ketone utilization, inhibiting Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger 1 and 3 (NHE1/NHE3), and suppressing renal/cardiac inflammation and fibrosis. GLP-1RAs act predominantly via anti-inflammatory pathways, endothelial protection, reduction of oxidative stress, inhibition of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, and attenuation of renal hyperfiltration via systemic anti-atherosclerotic pathways. Conclusion: SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs display distinct yet complementary molecular pathways. Their synergistic mechanism provides a strong rationale for combined therapy to achieve optimal cardiorenal protection in clinical practice.

items.title: MOLECULAR MECHANISMS UNDERLYING THE CARDIO- AND NEPHROPROTECTIVE EFFECTS OF SGLT2 INHIBITORS AND GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONISTS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW

items.summary: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
items.title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models

items.summary: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.
items.title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong

items.summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmar
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

items.summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.

items.summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.
tags: SAR interferometry; coherence; flood-risk mapping; detection power; insurance equity; canopy decoher
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of computed-Aperture Radar Interferometric Coherence for Computer Agriculture Flood-Risk Mapping Under Vegetation Canopy Decoherence: An Artificial Intelligence Detection-Power Bound for Insurance Payout Equity

items.summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; ac
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety

items.summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

items.summary: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $ΔΦ$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive--optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.
items.title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play

items.summary: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
items.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing

items.summary: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
items.title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory

items.summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound;
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
items.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories

items.summary: Description: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator used for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO₂ in inland waters. The firmware controls the water and gas pumps, reads a SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor and a DS18B20 water-temperature probe, and logs the data to an SD card with timestamps from a real-time clock. It accompanies the manuscript “A microcontroller-based, low-cost platform for continuous pCO₂ measurements in lakes and reservoirs” (Grochocki and Mannich, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods, under review). Hardware ·          Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) ·          SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor, 0–10,000 ppm (UART/Modbus via SoftwareSerial; RX pin 3, TX pin 2) ·          DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe (OneWire, pin 6) ·          DS1307 real-time clock (I²C) ·          SD card module (SPI, CS pin 10) ·          Two-channel relay module: water pump (pin 7) and gas pump (pin 5) Operating cycle 1.       Switch on the water and gas pumps. 2.       For the duration of a measurement cycle, read CO₂ and water temperature at a fixed interval and append each reading to a daily file on the SD card. 3.       Switch off both pumps and stay idle until the next cycle. Configuration Timing parameters are read at boot from a config.txt file on the SD card, one key=value per line: ·          measurementInterval : idle time between cycles (minutes) ·          dataCollectionInterval : time between readings (seconds) ·          fullMeasurementTime : duration of each cycle (minutes) If the file does not exist, the firmware creates one with default values, which take effect at the next boot. The values hard-coded in the sketch are a 10-min cycle, 5-s readings and a 45-min idle period. Output One comma-separated text file per day, named YY-MM-DD.txt , with the header Date Time, CO2 (ppm), Water Temp (C) . Timestamps are written as YYYY-M-D H:M:S , without zero padding. Each file is opened and closed at every write, so data are not lost if power is cut. Notes ·          The CO₂ values logged are the raw K30 output. Calibration against a reference analyzer, conversion to pCO₂ (water-vapor and pressure correction) and conversion to dissolved CO₂ are done in post-processing, as described in the accompanying paper (Eqs. 1–5). ·          If the RTC has not been set, it is set at first boot to the compile time of the sketch. ·          The K30 automatic baseline correction (ABC) assumes regular exposure to ~400 ppm air, so it should be disabled for underwater use. Required libraries: SD, SPI, Wire, SoftwareSerial (Arduino core); OneWire; DallasTemperature; TimeLib; DS1307RTC.
items.title: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO2
